content: Lesson 27 named three participles. Here
is the commonest use Latin makes of one.
An ABLATIVE ABSOLUTE is a noun and a
participle, both ablative, standing apart
from the sentence around them:
hīs rēbus cognitīs
= when this had been learned
urbe captā
= after the city was taken
Neither word belongs to the main clause.
They agree with nothing in it, and no
preposition governs them.
Graviōre sententiā prōnūntiātā,
supplicium sūmpsit.
= Once a heavier sentence had been
passed, he exacted the penalty.
Case alone marks it. English needs a
conjunction: when, after, once, since,
although. The story decides which; the
Latin does not say.
The participle sets the timing:
urbe captā     the city once taken
urbe ārdente   while the city burns
Some pairs carry no participle. esse has
none in the present, so a second noun
stands in its place:
Caesare duce   with Caesar as leader
mē cōnsule     in my consulship
Cover the pair with a thumb: what is left
still stands as a whole sentence. That
test is the whole skill.
Lesson 29 gave the passive of the present
system: -tur, -ntur. The perfect system
has no such endings. It uses two words.
A perfect passive participle, then a form
of sum:
captus est     he was taken
capta est      she was taken
captī sunt     they were taken
Hostium dux comprehēnsus est atque ad
Caesarem ductus.
= The enemy leader was seized and
taken to Caesar.
One est serves both participles here.
Latin drops the second freely, and the
reader supplies it.
est beside a participle is not a present
tense. captus est is 'he was taken', not
'he is taken'. The tense sits in sum:
captus est     was taken
captus erat    had been taken
captus erit    will have been taken
One participle, three tenses — the mirror
of Lesson 22's one stem, three tenses.
The participle stays an adjective, so it
agrees with the subject:
Hoc flāgitium grave iūdicātum est.
= This disgrace was judged serious.
Not every participle with sum is passive.
A deponent wears this build and keeps an
active sense: secūtus est, 'he followed'.
Some verbs wear the -r endings of Lesson
29 and mean something wholly active. They
are called DEPONENT, and no rule derives
them: they are known one by one.
imitor       I imitate
sequor       I follow
ūtor         I use
loquor       I speak
morior       I die
proficīscor  I set out
imitor never means 'I am imitated'. No
passive sense hides in the shape.
Eōs ego fortasse nunc imitor et ūtor
aetātis vitiō.
= Perhaps I am now imitating those
men, and indulging my years' fault.
The perfect comes in two words: the
participle and a form of sum. The build
is the passive's; the sense is not.
secūtus est    he followed
profectus est  he set out
oblītī sumus   we have forgotten
Their participles read active as well:
profectus = 'having set out'.
Several govern an odd case, and a card's
Notes name it on first meeting:
ūtor, fruor + ablative   vitiō
oblīvīscor + genitive    iniūriārum
The DEPONENT line on a card's Notes is
the warning: read the verb active.
